tier_reason: Public harness (bench.c, build.sh, ext/shim with image-png pinned as a submodule at 4ab5484, analyze.py) times ffpng and image-png in one process and memcmp-verifies every decoder's output against image-png as canonical RGBA8; compiler (gcc 16.1 / 16.2.1), full flags in build.sh and the shim's Cargo/rustflags, and CPUs (Ryzen 9 7950X, Ryzen 9 9950X3D, isolated core, boost off) are all stated. Both README tables (1.115x and 1.204x geomean, 13 categories) match the page exactly.

corrections.baseline: image-rs/image-png v0.18.1 (commit 4ab5484; the Rust png crate, already listed) built with --features=unstable at target-cpu=x86-64-v3. The same harness also times libpng + zlib, libspng, stb_image and ldpng (ffpng's front end with libdeflate inflate), but the README publishes no libpng, libspng or stb_image numbers
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1 (7950X run) and gcc 16.2.1 (9950X3D run) with -std=c99 -O2 -march=x86-64-v3 -mbmi -mbmi2 -mpclmul -falign-functions=32 -falign-loops=64:47 -funroll-all-loops -fno-plt -fwrapv -fno-stack-protector -fno-pie -fcf-protection=none -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -fno-unwind-tables -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables (build.sh). image-png via cargo +nightly release build with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort and rustflags target-cpu=x86-64-v3 (ext/shim/Cargo.toml, ext/shim/.cargo/config.toml); the nightly is named only for the follow-up (1.98.0-nightly c1b22f44c). README says clang builds of ffpng run about 10% slower
corrections.caveats: The win is over image-png (the previous fastest decoder), not over libpng: the harness times libpng, libspng and stb_image but the README prints no numbers for them, so no libpng speedup is stated. Output semantics are image-png's EXPAND | STRIP_16 (16-bit truncated to 8 bits), not libpng default output; equivalence is checked byte for byte after conversion to RGBA8, outside the timed loop, and mismatching images are excluded from the aggregate (both README runs report all 2848 images passing). The timed region includes per-decode allocation for both decoders (image-png's shim allocates a zeroed Vec; ffpng mallocs). ffpng checks critical-chunk CRCs and, like image-png's default, does not verify the zlib Adler-32 (no Adler code in ffpng.h). The shim source comment still says target-cpu=native while .cargo/config.toml sets x86-64-v3 (stale comment). Corpus (QOI benchmark suite, about 1.1 GB) is downloaded, not vendored. Absolute throughput depends on core isolation and boost off; the ratio is the stable figure. Very new single-author repository (first commit 2026-06-23, 0 stars). Every source file carries an SPDX MIT tag and a copyright line, but the repository has no LICENSE file. x86-64-v3 only (AVX2, BMI2, PCLMUL); decode only, no encoder.

notes: Strong, careful harness: same-process interleaved timing, per-image ratio, oracle check against image-png. The baseline is the already-listed image-png, so baseline_in_list is now true; the libpng comparison stays unpublished.

tier_reason: docs/benchmark-current.md numbers match the record; the encode matrix is produced by the public benchmark/run-large-matrix.ps1 (QLIC pack --threads 1, cjxl -d 0 -e 9 --num_threads=0, cwebp -lossless -exact -z 6, one pinned logical processor, rotated order, ImageMagick compare -metric AE must be 0 for every file), with JPEG XL efforts in run-jxl-efforts.ps1 and decode timing (one untimed run, then three pinned runs) in quick-benchmark.ps1; corpus pinned by URL, size and SHA-256 in downloads.json; compiler (Clang 22.1.4), Release flags (CMakeLists.txt) and CPU (Ryzen 9 9950X3D) are stated. Gaps noted in caveats: baseline binary versions are not on the current page, and the OxiPNG row has no public script.

corrections.baseline: JPEG XL lossless via stock cjxl (-d 0 -e 9 --num_threads=0) and WebP lossless via stock cwebp (-lossless -exact -z 6), per benchmark/run-large-matrix.ps1; the page also lists JPEG XL efforts 1-8, WebP presets 1-9 and an OxiPNG level 6 row. No PNG or QOI decoder is a baseline
corrections.compiler_and_flags: QLIC: published portable x86-64 build from Clang 22.1.4 (clang-cl), Release options from CMakeLists.txt: /O2 /Oi /Ot /Gy /Gw plus /clang:-O3, ThinLTO on the qlic target, codec/src/map_avx2.c compiled with /arch:AVX2; no -march=native, no PGO. Baselines: stock cjxl and cwebp binaries whose versions the current page does not state (the older docs/benchmark-0.5-historical.json names cwebp 1.6.0 and cjxl 0.12.0 with the same command lines); OxiPNG version and command line not stated
corrections.claimed_speedup: Encode (one pinned logical processor, wall time including process startup and file I/O): QLIC 618.673 s vs JPEG XL lossless effort 9 5,674.173 s (about 9.2x faster, derived from page data) with a 0.30% smaller total (1,160,913,984 vs 1,164,424,898 bytes, per page). Against JPEG XL effort 5 (629.126 s, 1,230,084,951 bytes) encode time is about equal and QLIC output is 5.6% smaller (derived from page data). Against WebP lossless preset 6 (585.964 s) QLIC is about 5.6% slower but 9.97% smaller (page). OxiPNG level 6 took 9,105.634 s (about 14.7x slower than QLIC, derived from page data), but no public script runs OxiPNG. Decode (one untimed run, then the average of three pinned process runs per file, each including process startup and writing a PNG output): QLIC 236.927 s (8.291 MP/s) vs JPEG XL effort 9 files 307.602 s (6.386 MP/s, 29.83% slower per page, so QLIC about 1.30x faster, derived) but WebP preset 6 files 117.887 s (16.663 MP/s), about 2.0x faster than QLIC (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Single-author benchmark of a three-month-old project, Windows 11 only, one run. The 9.2x encode win is against JPEG XL effort 9, an extreme setting: at effort 5 encode time is similar and QLIC is 5.6% smaller, and JPEG XL efforts 1 to 4 and WebP presets 1 to 6 encode faster than QLIC but produce 10% to 33% larger output (derived from page data). QLIC encodes at only about 3.2 MP/s (derived), so it is a ratio-at-speed (Pareto) entry rather than a fast codec, and WebP decodes about 2x faster. Encode and decode wall times include process startup and file I/O; decode times also include each tool's own PNG writer for the output file, so the decode comparison partly measures three different PNG encoders. Baseline binary versions are not stated on the current page (the 0.5 historical record names cwebp 1.6.0 and cjxl 0.12.0); the OxiPNG row is not produced by any script in benchmark/; per-file results and the run summary.json are kept in a private development workspace, not in the repository. build.ps1 picks a Visual Studio generator without selecting clang-cl, so reproducing the Clang build needs a manual toolset choice. Release 1.0.1 (2026-09-12) fixed an encoder bug that could write an invalid 32-byte file for large palettes; the benchmark's exact-decode check would have stopped on such a file, so the published totals are not affected. Repository code is C (CMake project LANGUAGES C), not C++.

notes: Language should be C (CMakeLists.txt: project(qlic ... LANGUAGES C)); language is not a correctable field here, so the orchestrator may want an override. A is borderline: the harness, QLIC build flags, CPU and exact-pixel verification are public, but baseline tool versions for the current run are only implied by the older 0.5 record.

tier_reason: First-party numbers only: lowzag's peak_alloc figures are reproducible (pinned in CI by test/check_docs.py through lowzag_estimate on a generated 4000x3000 corpus file), but the libjpeg 36.1 MB figure is computed from 282,000 blocks x 128-byte JBLOCK, the process peak RSS table in docs/ALGORITHM.md (lowzag CLI vs djpeg, libjpeg-turbo 3.0.4) names no CPU model, compiler or script, and the ESP32-S3 timing table is three single measurements from one board with no harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Memory at 12 MP 4:2:0 progressive: lowzag peak_alloc 36.2, 19.6, 6.8 and 3.4 MB at scales 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 against libjpeg-turbo's 36.1 MB coefficient array at every scale (about 10.6x less at 1/8, derived from page data); with an 800x480 crop 3.4, 2.8, 2.4 and 2.3 MB. Measured process peak RSS (ru_maxrss, lowzag CLI vs djpeg -nosmooth, libjpeg-turbo 3.0.4 on aarch64, docs/ALGORITHM.md): 36,580 vs 36,876 KiB at 1/1, 23,648 vs 36,980 at 1/2, 9,916 vs 36,552 at 1/4, 4,636 vs 36,536 at 1/8 (about 7.9x less at 1/8, derived from page data). Decode time on ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz, lowzag on the progressive file vs ROM TJpgDec on a jpegtran-converted baseline file with the same pixels: 4000x3000 at 1/4 5.7 s vs 9.1 s (about 1.6x faster, derived), 1600x1200 at 1/2 1.75 s vs 1.95 s, 800x480 at 1/1 0.63 s vs 0.46 s (lowzag slower).
corrections.hardware: ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz (timing table); unnamed aarch64 machine for the RSS table; peak_alloc figures are allocation sizes from lowzag's own sizing code, not tied to a CPU
corrections.caveats: A memory win, not a speed win, and a weak fit for a speed list. The headline table compares two different quantities (lowzag's info.peak_alloc against the coefficient array size libjpeg-turbo requests, computed from its 128-byte JBLOCK), as the README says; a separate measured RSS table in docs/ALGORITHM.md supports the gap (7.9x at 1/8, derived) but gives no CPU model, compiler or script. Memory still scales with source size (8-byte map per source block, 2.26 MB floor at 12 MP). The speed table compares different work: lowzag decodes a progressive file while ROM TJpgDec decodes the baseline-format version of it, and TJpgDec's 1/2 and 1/4 modes run the full IDCT; the figures are single measurements from one board, not reproducible on a host, and at 800x480 TJpgDec is faster. There is no host speed comparison against libjpeg-turbo. Progressive (SOF2, Huffman) JPEG only. Development is on a self-hosted GitLab with GitHub as a mirror (1 star). Commits list an AI co-author (Claude). The claim that mozjpeg, stb_image, Go image/jpeg and Rust jpeg-decoder also size progressive coefficient storage from the source dimensions comes from source reading (docs/PRIOR-ART.md), not measurement.

notes: Record numbers are accurate; I added the measured RSS table and labelled the TJpgDec comparison as progressive-vs-baseline-format work. Keep at C as a memory-metric entry with a weak-fit shortcoming.
